source.title: An Overview of Compact Star Populations and Some of Its Open Problems

accepted.question_text: Do neutron-star magnetic fields genuinely decay over astrophysical timescales, and if so do they fade almost completely within about 10^6 years or instead decay only partially to a persistent 'bottom field' that remains substantial even in very old systems such as black widows?

evidence.quote: This question is one of the oldest, and has been answered differently over the years. The idea that there must be a decay of the field within ∼106 yr is quite popular
Magnetic fields may decay partially to a “bottom field”, but not completely

accepted.question_text: What evolutionary relationships connect the observed neutron-star subpopulations, including ordinary radio pulsars, central compact objects, X-ray Dim Isolated Neutron Stars (XDINSs), Rotating Radio Transients (RRATs), magnetars, and other hidden neutron stars, and which of these classes are genuinely distinct populations versus temporary evolutionary stages of the same underlying objects?

evidence.quote: most of the Galactic NSs are not pulsars, but instead belong to one of several classes that may be termed “hidden”, which we describe below
These include the central compact objects (CCOs)
the subpopulation termed the Magnificent Seven or X-ray Dim Isolated Neutron Stars (XDINSs)
Another subpopulation which was identified unexpectedly is that of Rotating Radio Transients (RRATs)
A third subgroup of importance is that of the so-called magnetars
Which is the relationship between all these subpopulations?
The idea that some subpopulations are just an evolutionary stage leading to some other type is behind all the attempts of unification

accepted.question_text: Are the recently discovered ultra-slow magnetars and other very long-period neutron-star candidates simply older evolutionary stages of magnetars that have cooled and spun down to extremely long periods, or are they a distinct population, possibly closer in nature to RRATs than to standard magnetar evolution?

evidence.quote: The latest news about the NSs population include the discovery of progressively longer period pulsars [46] and magnetars [12]
Are the new objects old magnetars?
The ultra-slow magnetars should be, logically thinking, a latter stage in which they have cooled and braked to very long periods.
Is there a real difference between RRATs and ultra-slow magnetars?

accepted.question_text: Does the compact-object mass distribution contain a true lower black-hole mass gap between about 2 and 5 solar masses, or is that interval only partially depleted, with some objects and formation channels populating at least part of the 2.5–5 solar-mass range?

evidence.quote: its existence has remained an open question for over 20 years
The gap has been connected to the characteristic convection timescale in core-collapse supernovae [26,27], but even in this case a partial filling has not been ruled out.

It seems thus clear at this point that, if there is a gap, it should not start below ∼2.5 M☉, and that the investigation of alternative formation channels for compact objects is needed to further constrain the degree to which the 2.5–5 M☉ range is populated.
